title: A color palette a founder can remember
metaTitle: A palette a founder can name
excerpt: Paper, ink, a line, and one accent. If the founder cannot name the colors, the next slide and the next screen will invent new ones.
alt: An OPEN sign hanging in a shop window, with the word SHOP printed on the glass. The simple sign fits a piece about a color palette small enough to remember.
caption: Four roles are easier to keep than a drawer of swatches. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How many colors does a startup palette need?
faqs.answer: Four roles are enough: paper for the background, ink for text, a line for edges and dividers, and one accent for the action. Status colors such as danger and success can sit beside that list, and they should not reuse the accent. If the founder cannot name the roles, the list is already too long.

faqs.question: What contrast should the palette meet?
faqs.answer: WCAG 2.2 asks for at least 4.5 to 1 between normal text and its background, and 3 to 1 for large text. Meaningful interface parts, such as an input border, need about 3 to 1 against the adjacent color. Check the accent as a button and as text. A color that fails those pairs needs a narrower job, not a quieter body font.

faqs.question: How do you stop a deck from inventing new colors?
faqs.answer: Ship a template whose picker only contains paper, ink, the line, and the accent. Remove the extra swatches. New colors tend to start in slides and then leak into the product. A proposed color has to replace an existing role or it stays out.

markdown:
A startup color palette a founder can remember has four roles: paper, ink, a line, and one accent. If the founder cannot name the colors, the next slide and the next screen will invent new ones. The palette is a memory aid before it is a brand system.

Write the names in ordinary words. Then attach the values. The names are what get reused in a deck at midnight. The values are what keep the interface honest.

## Paper, ink, a line, and one accent

Paper is the background. It can be warm white, cool white, or a deep color if the whole product is dark, but it is one surface the work sits on. A second paper, slightly different, can lift a card. That is elevation, and it is still paper. It is not a new brand color.

Ink is the text. One ink for body and headings, and a quieter ink for secondary sentences if you truly need it. Two inks is the limit for a small team. A third gray will be used as a fourth, because nobody remembers the difference between gray-500 and gray-600 under pressure.

The line draws boxes, dividers, and input edges. It is usually ink at low strength, or a mix of ink and paper. Give it a name. "Border" is a job. "Gray-200" is a value someone will replace with gray-300 because the screen looked a little flat.

The accent is the one color that is not paper or ink. It marks the primary action, the current item, and a link if links are not simply ink with an underline. It does not mark every icon, every heading, and every chart series. When the accent is everywhere, nothing is accented. You are back to a single color, plus fatigue.

That is the whole palette a founder needs to recite: paper, ink, line, accent. If they can point at a screen and name those four, the next person who opens a slide can match it. If they cannot, they will pick a blue they like that week, and the product will follow the slide.

## Name them so a tired person can repeat them

The names should be sayable. Paper, ink, line, accent. Or canvas, ink, rule, signal. Pick one set and keep it. "Brand primary 600" does not survive a conversation. "The blue" does, until you have two blues.

Write one sentence for each role, the way you would brief a new teammate. "Paper is the page. Ink is anything you read. The line separates. The accent is the thing you can press." Put those sentences on the first page of the brand note, above the hex values. Values without jobs are a menu.

Show the four in a row, as large swatches, with a sentence of interface under them: a button in the accent, a paragraph in ink, a card on paper, a field outlined by the line. A palette that has only been seen as circles on a white artboard has not been seen. The founder should recognize it inside a screen, not only inside the guideline.

If you need status colors, add them as a separate short list: danger, success, warning. They are not the accent. A product that uses the accent for errors will train people to ignore both. Three status colors, named, with a light and a text pair each, is enough. Do not build a traffic-light system you use once.

Neutrals beyond paper, ink, and line are where palettes bloat. Before you add a gray, ask which role is missing. If the answer is "the card looks nicer," try a second paper first. If the answer is "this text should be quieter," try the secondary ink you already named. Add a swatch only when a role exists.

## Contrast is part of the name

A color the founder loves still has to be readable. The W3C's [WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the door into WCAG 2.2, the shared standard for web content. Normal text needs a contrast of at least 4.5 to 1 against its background. Large text can meet 3 to 1. Parts of the interface that carry meaning, such as an input's edge or an icon button, need about 3 to 1 against the color next to them.

Check ink on paper, accent as text on paper, and accent as a button with its label. A bright accent often fails as a button fill with white text, or it fails as a text link on paper. When that happens, keep the accent for fills and icons that pass, and use ink for text links with an underline. Do not solve a failed ratio by making the body text the accent. You will have painted the page in the action color.

Disabled and placeholder are the tempting exceptions. They still have to be legible. If a placeholder is doing the job of a label, it is ink, and it owes 4.5 to 1. Quiet is allowed for a hint that sits under a real label. Invisible is not a role.

If you ship a dark theme, the four roles get a second value each. The names stay. Paper becomes the dark surface, ink becomes the light text, the line is redrawn so it shows, and the accent is adjusted until it passes on the dark paper. A filter that inverts the light palette is not that work. Check the pairs. Write both values under the same name.

## Where the palette is allowed to show up

The website, the product, and the deck share the four roles. They do not share every layout. A marketing page can use more paper and a larger accent button. The product can use more line and less accent. The ratio of use can change. The colors cannot.

Slides are where palettes go to die. A template with paper, ink, line, and accent, and no other swatches in the picker, will be used. A template that includes the full spectrum "for flexibility" will be used in full. Remove the extra swatches. Flexibility is how the Tuesday deck invents a teal the product does not have.

Charts are the other leak. Give a chart one accent and ink, plus a pattern or a label when a series must be distinguished. A six-color chart is a second palette. If you truly have six series, label them and use ink at full and quiet strengths before you reach for new hues. New hues will escape the chart and land on a status pill.

Photography sits on the paper. It does not replace the palette. A campaign image full of red does not mean the accent becomes red for the quarter. Frame the photo so the interface around it can stay itself. The palette is the thing that should still be true when the campaign is over.

Illustration, if you use it, borrows the same four. A drawing with its own mint and peach is a palette amendment done in secret. Send it back. The system is small on purpose.

## How you hand it to the team

One page is the delivery. The four names, the sentences, the values for light and for dark if dark exists, and one screen that uses only those roles. A second page can show the status pairs and the things you refuse: no extra grays, no accent on body text, no new color in slides.

Engineers need the names in code. CSS variables or a small theme file, with `--paper`, `--ink`, `--line`, `--accent`. Designers need the same names in Figma variables. If the names diverge, the colors will diverge a week later. Someone will "just pick a close one" because matching hex by eye felt faster than finding the source.

The client portal is a good home for the page and the source file, next to the logo. A palette pasted into a chat will be screenshotted, and the screenshot will be wrong six months later when you adjust the accent to pass contrast. The latest page is the one that matters. Say that on the page itself, with a date.

When a new color is proposed, the question is which role it replaces. If it replaces none, it does not enter. That sentence is the whole governance a team of five needs. A color committee is how a startup palette becomes a brand book nobody opens.

## A test you can do from memory

Close the file. Ask the founder to name the colors. Then open the product and the last sales deck.

- They can say paper, ink, line, and accent without looking.
- The deck uses only those.
- Body text meets 4.5 to 1 on paper.
- The accent is the action, not the paragraph.
- Dark, if it exists, uses the same four names with new values.
- Code and Figma share the names.

If the founder names seven colors, you do not have a palette yet. You have a collection. Cut it back to four roles and let the screens get simpler. The product will feel more like itself when there is less to remember.

Type is the next choice that either supports this or argues with it. [Type pairing for a site and a product](/blog/type-pairing-for-a-site-and-a-product) is the next piece. One family can do both jobs. If you use two, write down which one is for headlines and which one is for the interface.

You can see palettes held to a small set in finished projects. Look through [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) and notice how few colors a clear page actually needs. The constraint is the craft.
